claims.text: An optimal Ta content promotes formation of a dominant CrTaO4-based oxide scale in refractory CrTa-containing high-entropy alloys.
The resulting CrTaO4-based oxide scale is dense, adherent, and self-limiting.
A dominant CrTaO4-based scale retards oxygen ingress.
Retarding oxygen ingress through this scale provides superior high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The refractory elements are initially distributed uniformly in the baseline alloy.
Changing Ta content and associated refractory-element levels can promote or suppress formation of a CrTaO4-based scale.
Oxidation behavior is governed by the relative oxidation free energies of Cr and Ta.
At an optimal Ta content, the thermodynamic balance favors formation of stable, adherent CrTaO4.
CrTaO4 acts as an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Without an optimal Ta balance, competing oxides form and are less protective.
An optimized-Ta alloy will develop a dense, slow-growing CrTaO4-based oxide layer during oxidation at 1000–1100°C.
Growth of the protective scale will produce parabolic mass-gain kinetics.
Alloys with reduced or excessive Ta will develop rapidly growing, non-protective oxide scales.
The non-optimized-Ta baseline does not form a dominant protective CrTaO4-based scale.
The proposed mechanism applies to refractory high-entropy alloys oxidized at 1000–1100°C for extended durations.
The mechanism may not extend to lower temperatures or fundamentally different alloy systems.
Multiple oxide phases may form simultaneously in multicomponent alloys, complicating attribution of protection uniquely to CrTaO4.
Failure of the optimized-Ta alloy to show both a significantly slower oxidation rate and a predominant CrTaO4 scale relative to the reduced-Ta control would falsify the hypothesis.
